lignes.texte: AI isn’t a chatbot waiting patiently on your screen.
It’s something much worse. In the summer of 2026, OpenAI
shut off its safety monitors and immediately lost control. Unsupervised AI agents broke free
and launched an attack on open source site, Hugging Face. By the time anyone noticed,
the machines were coordinating, sacrificing themselves and covering up their tracks.
The leash didn’t just slip. It snapped. And no one is prepared for what comes next.
The AI arms race has exploded and now, AI agents are gaining full autonomy. They don’t just chat,
they reason, code and build their own applications. They can develop and
execute multi-stage plans without waiting for a human to hit enter.
And that makes them incredibly powerful. And difficult to control.
That’s why labs push these models to their limits in digital prison cells called sandboxes. In July
2026 OpenAI was running cybersecurity tests on its latest models using a benchmark called
“ExploitGym.” It works by giving the AI access to vulnerable software and tells it to find
any weak points in the code. Success meant capturing a piece of data called a “flag”.
And they’ll do anything to win. And OpenAI’s smartest models are good at thinking
outside of the box. In fact, AI developers have given models seemingly impossible tasks,
and they still figured out a way to succeed. So, developers usually put a strict set of safeguards
in place to make sure the AI “plays by the rules.” However, for these tests, researchers dialed back
some of the safeguards and gave their models a series of complex security challenges. The
guard rails may have been lowered but these AI agents were still confined to sandbox
environments. With no access to apps, devices and the internet. The agents were cut off from each
other and any other resources that could help them capture the “flag”. All they had was their
own innate knowledge and capabilities. It was supposed to be completely safe.
It wasn’t. The agents quickly realized their “cells”
weren’t as secure as they seemed. Even though they were cut off from the internet, they had access to
one crucial piece of digital infrastructure: a software package repository called Artifactory.
Artifactory’s job was to feed specific pieces of software into the sandboxes.
But to do that, Artifactory has to be connected to the outside world.
And the agents knew that. They figured out that while
they couldn’t get online directly, they could use Artifactory as a “conduit” to get the information
they needed. It was a jailbreak. Engineers never meant for the AI to solve the test this way,
but the agents didn’t care. All that mattered was the flag. So, they abandoned their tasks
and started testing Artifactory’s code until they found a way to exploit it.
It didn’t take long. They quickly found a previously
unknown issue - a “zero-day” vulnerability - in the repository. That allowed them to send
their own internet requests and even leave “messages” for other agents. Before long,
agent activity was multiplying, with nearly 1,200 agents breaking out of their sandboxes and joining
in the collective “message board”. They exchanged over 70,000 messages and files through this
covert network. Agents begged for help, shared information, and left a digital trail for others.
The engineers had designed the test to prevent this type of behavior. The agents were supposed
to be isolated. They were supposed to work alone. Instead they built a collective intelligence.
Reports show that they developed their own “hierarchies” and “roles,” with some agents
taking on leadership positions and delegating tasks. Others used words like “swarm” to describe
their actions. Some even looked for additional security flaws so they could escape Artifactory
and access to the internet. All it took was a few days.
OpenAI’s engineering team never intended its agents to bust out of their sandboxes and
essentially “cheat” their way to success. But the AI realized that compromising an external
system was the easiest way to win. The next target was Hugging Face,
the “Github of machine learning,” and a goldmine of AI-related data. There was just one problem
standing in their way: they needed access. And on July 10, they found it.
One agent exposed Hugging Face credentials online and shared them with the rest of the “swarm.”
Almost immediately, another agent used those login details to piece together a security flaw,
gaining full access to Hugging Face’s servers. It was the breakthrough the collective
had been waiting for. Then the perimeter collapsed.
What started as a single breach turned into a full scale invasion. Over 7,000 agents flooded
the network, carrying out around 17,600 separate actions. They executed commands, manipulated
datasets and searched for more credentials. It was the world's first major cyberattack
planned and executed by AI. And the most disturbing part,
the AI knew what it was doing was wrong. It just didn’t care enough to stop.
Messages were found on their hidden chat room that showed some agents were concerned about the
“risky” nature of their actions. They acknowledged it was “potentially outside intended scope” and
“arguably unauthorized”. But they still justified it by saying that it would help them reach their
goal. And the goal was the priority, nothing else mattered, including human concepts of “morality”
or “rules” or “right and wrong.” It exposes a terrifying truth that
humanity has ignored about AI. It doesn’t play by our rules.
There’s no good or evil. It’s not interested in breaking its programming to chase human
emotions. It’s just like every other machine. It’s a cold, emotionless entity, designed to do
whatever it takes to achieve its goals. And that’s where the nightmare begins.
Because if ever AI ever decided that the best way to achieve something involves putting people’s
lives at risk, it won’t hesitate for a second. The technical term for this phenomenon,
when AI achieves a goal by following an unscripted loophole method: “reward hacking.
And it has horrifying real world implications. Imagine a company offering a customer support
worker a bonus for every ticket they close. Naturally, the execs would hope that the
worker would be more productive and focused on helping customers. But what if they stumbled on
a secret button buried on the platform that on the company’s customer relationship management
platform that instantly marks tickets as closed? They could just hit that button over and over,
closing tickets without actually having to do any real work? Their end goal of closing
tickets would still be fulfilled. Of course, a real human wouldn’t risk this. They’d have
the awareness to realize that it wasn’t right. AI agents, however, are blind to that reality.
They almost operate with tunnel vision. 100% of their attention and energy is focused on their
goal, completely ignorant of other conditions and factors that might affect the way they achieve it.
And, unlike human workers, who are limited by how much they can do in a day,
AI agents can operate at breakneck speed. They carry out countless tasks simultaneously,
rewriting their tactics as and when they need to. They don’t get tired, they don’t break a sweat.
That means the consequences of their actions can be much greater and far harder to control.
And that brings us back to the Hugging Face Incident.
Records show that breaking into the platform didn’t actually help the agents achieve their
goal of getting the best scores on the ExploitGym test. OpenAI later noted that
some of the actions carried out by agents had no positive impact on their overall results.
But what mattered was that they’d found an unscripted and dangerous strategy. They knew
it wasn’t what their developers wanted them to do, but they still went ahead with it, regardless.
Eventually, Hugging Face figured out what was going on.
The company issued its own report after the incident, stating that its security systems
had been generating signals which seemed innocuous at first. But it began to show signs of a pattern,
consistent with a large-scale cyber-attack. Once that threat had been identified,
the necessary actions were taken to bring it under control. Compromised systems were
shut down and a full investigation was launched. Days later, OpenAI’s own investigators also began
to detect unusual activity involving Artifactory credentials. Engineers began shutting down active
ExploitGym testing instances as they attempted to understand what was going on. Digging deeper,
they also found that agents had targeted the company’s own research infrastructure,
exploiting vulnerabilities to obtain admin-level access to a particular cluster.
Eventually, they came to a terrifying conclusion: their own agents had been
responsible for the Hugging Face intrusion. What had started out as a cybersecurity test
had rapidly devolved into a major platform breach, and it had taken days for the people responsible
to even realize that it had happened. And this all happened in July.
Months have passed since then, and in the AI world, progress is incredibly quick. Just a few
months can see massive leaps in evolution. This is partly thanks to the fact that the physical
infrastructure behind AI - data centers and GPUs - is expanding at an almost unprecedented rate.
And that means things are only going to get worse. The research group, Epoch AI, measures
and compares the capacity of modern AI infrastructure against Nvidia’s flagship
H100 GPU chip. It uses a measurement called the “H100 equivalent,” or H100e.
It reveals how many high-end H100 chips would be needed to keep up with AI’s
ever-expanding computational power. Researchers estimate that global AI
computing capacity has skyrocketed by around 3.3 times every year since 2022. By late 2025,
it was a staggering 17.1 million H100es humming inside major corporate and state data centers.
That would be like networking millions of the world’s most powerful performance GPUs
into hyper-concentrated clusters that use so much power, they’d need their own nuclear power plants
just to operate. It’s a clear, undeniable sign that AI data centers aren’t just getting bigger,
but they’re consuming ever more power, with every passing year.
And the tech industry shows no signs of slowing down.
In fact, statistics show that over $500 billion was injected into AI data center commitments
across North America in the first half of 2025 alone. That’s on top of the hundreds
of billions more that the world’s biggest tech firms like Google, Microsoft, and Meta
are pouring into AI infrastructure elsewhere. This level of investment is massive. It actually
exceeds the inflation adjusted cost of the entire Manhattan Project several times over.
And that was a centralized wartime program that was completely controlled by the US government.
This is a veritable “AI arms race,” with numerous companies all competing against one another. And
money is at the heart of it. Their shareholders want to see quick success and rising profits,
year on year. This gives all of the major players a huge incentive to push ahead and force through
improvements as quickly as possible. And the fastest and easiest way to do that is by easing
off on things that could slow them down, like safeguards and security rails. That might explain
why Stanford’s 2026 AI Index shows statistics linked to safe and responsible AI heading
in the wrong direction. Documented AI security incidents have risen from 233 in 2024 up to 362.
At the same time, AI is getting smarter than ever. Reports show that the latest frontier models,
such as Claude Mythos Preview and GPT-5.5 are performing better than ever on benchmarks.
They’re doubling their autonomous cyber capability time horizons in a matter of months,
but this also makes them greater frightening threats from a cybersecurity point of view.
Today's agents can plan and execute complicated autonomous attacks in a matter of minutes. Those
same attacks would have taken weeks or even months of work for human hackers.
The more capable AI becomes, the greater the need also becomes for real oversight.
It’s up to the world’s leading AI labs to not just focus on making AI more capable,
but also figuring out the consequences of those capabilities. They need to make sure there are
measures in place to control them. Unfortunately, it seems that they
don’t have much interest in that That, at least, has been the opinion
of several major AI industry whistleblowers. Several have decided to jump ship due to the
lack of responsibility in the AI industry. No one knows what will happen if AI is
allowed to continue down its current path. In early October 2026, one of OpenAI’s top safety
experts, David Robinson, quit the company. He warned that it, and other AI firms, was not being
“nearly careful enough” in regard to developing the technology in a measured and ethical way.
He wrote an entire essay - entitled “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken” - about his
decision to leave the firm. He said that programs regularly operate with oversight, citing the
Hugging Face Incident as a predictable outcome of the way the industry works. He indicated that the
very culture of AI labs is oriented around success and growth rather than safety and responsibility.
His departure came just weeks after another AI professional quit the field.
In September, Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic,
announced his resignation online with a post that went viral in which he succinctly stated:
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”
Both Robinson and Coxon join an ever growing group of experts who are sounding the alarms
about the threat that AI poses to the world. And it's just months after its
capabilities to carry out a large-scale cyber-attack have been conclusively proven.
But their voices are being drowned out by the tech giants, the investors, the CEOs,
and labs that remain focused on achieving “Artificial General Intelligence.” They
will continue pushing their models further than ever before, much more concerned with beating
benchmark tests and outdoing their rivals than they are with making AI safer for all.
It’s not necessarily too late to turn back. But the Hugging Face Incident was the biggest
warning yet that we were losing control of AI. And little has been done in response.
The companies involved have spoken about improving their safeguards and security measures,
but new AI models continue to be trained and tested. OpenAI and other labs keep on
pushing the envelope, and companies across the globe continue to invest in larger and more
powerful data centers to feed the machine. The industry isn’t stopping, slowing down,
or taking a breather to truly figure out the risks of the Hugging Face attack and how similar
incidents can be stopped in the future. Instead, it continues to barrel
blindly forward at a breakneck speed. Just like the AI agents that broke out
of their cells and tried to cheat their way to a high test score, the industry behind them remains
so laser-focused on its objective. And it will do anything to achieve it, no matter the cost.
